fields.before: Seven steps the immune system must complete to kill a tumour: release of antigens, pick-up by dendritic cells, priming of T cells in lymph nodes, travel, entry into the tumour, recognition, and killing. Every immunotherapy pushes on one step; every escape blocks one.
fields.after: The cancer-immunity cycle maps linked steps from available tumour antigens to T-cell recognition and killing. It helps locate a question or bottleneck; a result at one step does not establish the whole response.

fields.before: Chen and Mellman's cycle: (1) dying tumour cells release neoantigens; (2) dendritic cells (BATF3+ cDC1) capture and cross-present them; (3) in lymph nodes, T cells are primed via TCR-MHC plus CD28-B7, with CTLA-4 as the brake; (4) effector T cells traffic via CXCL9/10-CXCR3; (5) infiltrate through vasculature and stroma; (6) recognise peptide-MHC-I; (7) kill via perforin/granzyme and IFN-γ, releasing more antigen. Each step has failure modes (low antigenicity, poor DC function, Treg-dominated priming, abnormal vessels, TGF-β stroma, MHC loss, PD-1 exhaustion) and matching drugs (radiation, STING agonists and vaccines for 1-2; anti-CTLA-4 for 3; anti-VEGF for 4-5; engagers and CAR-T bypass 6; anti-PD-1 for 7).
fields.after:
Chen and Mellman’s 2013 framework describes seven linked steps: release of cancer antigens; their collection and presentation; T-cell priming and activation; trafficking; entry into tumour tissue; recognition of cancer cells; and killing. Further antigen release may support another round. In conventional T-cell recognition, a displayed peptide-HLA complex and a suitable T-cell receptor are separate dependencies.

This is a T-cell-centred organizing model, not a universal route, assay result or treatment-selection algorithm. Steps overlap, priming may occur away from the tumour, and other immune mechanisms require their own account. Checkpoints and local tissue conditions affect several steps. Vaccines aim to generate or expand reactive responses, checkpoint drugs interrupt selected inhibitory signals, and engineered cells provide a recognition system and effectors. Each still needs appropriate targets, access, function and safety evidence.

after: In a fictional vaccine study, blood cells release a cytokine after added-peptide stimulation. This supports reactivity under that assay’s conditions. Added peptide can bypass natural processing, and the result does not establish entry into the sampled tumour, recognition of naturally presenting cancer cells, useful killing or clinical benefit. Antigen release is not priming, blood expansion is not infiltration, and a return arrow does not demonstrate durable protection.

Use the cycle to name the measured step and the next untested dependency. A proposed bottleneck or complementary pair of mechanisms does not establish a beneficial or safe combination. Increasing a response can also affect healthy tissue; the model does not identify a safe intervention by itself.

fields.before: A relay of seven runners. The race is only won if every baton is passed. Cancers usually drop only one or two batons, so the treatment that works is the one that fixes the step that actually failed, which is why the same drug cures one patient and does nothing for the next.
fields.after: A relay helps organize the questions: material must be available, presented, recognized and acted on. Several dependencies can be impaired together, and improving one handoff does not establish completion of the response. The map does not predict which treatment will help an individual.

Vaccines and antigen-presenting-cell approaches investigate antigen presentation and priming. The framework locates proposed jobs; it does not establish that a particular intervention completes them.

fields.before: 'Hot' tumours are full of immune cells and respond to immunotherapy; 'cold' tumours have kept the immune system out.
fields.after: Hot, excluded and desert describe where specified immune cells were found in sampled tissue. Their location alone does not establish tumour recognition, effective killing or benefit from a particular drug.

fields.before: Hot tumours are full of immune cells and tend to respond to immunotherapy, whereas cold tumours have kept the immune system out. Immunologists distinguish inflamed tumours, immune-excluded tumours in which T cells are held at the margin by TGF-β and stroma, and immune deserts. Pancreatic cancer, prostate cancer, glioblastoma and most HR-positive breast cancers are cold, and turning cold tumours hot is the goal of radiation, vaccines, ISACs, STING agonists and oncolytic viruses. The term is linked to the Immune checkpoint inhibitors, STING & innate immune agonists and Oncolytic viruses technologies and to Desmoplasia (tumour stroma), and it is referenced by the Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma and Glioma & glioblastoma entries, Miriam Merad and the bottleneck on cold tumours.
fields.after:
An inflamed or hot pattern has specified immune cells within sampled tumour regions. In an excluded pattern, cells concentrate in surrounding stroma or at a boundary with less entry into malignant nests. A desert has few relevant cells in the examined regions. Cold is used for desert alone or for both desert and excluded patterns, so state the definition. A macrophage-rich sample is not automatically T-cell inflamed.

These are observations about identity and location. Some infiltrating T cells recognize viral or other non-cancer antigens; others restrain responses. Region, specimen, disease site and sampling time matter, and treatment can change the pattern. Neither a small biopsy nor a pattern label describes every site in a person or selects an immunotherapy. Exclusion suggests questions about recruitment, vessels, matrix and local cells, rather than proving one causal wall.

before: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma is the archetypal cold tumour: T cells exist but are held at the margin by CXCL12 from FAP-positive fibroblasts (Feig 2013) and MHC class I is degraded by autophagy (Yamamoto 2020), so single-agent ipilimumab (0 of 27), anti-PD-L1 (0 of 14 pancreatic patients) and durvalumab with or without tremelimumab (3.1% and 0% of 65) all failed; the only responsive group is the 1 to 2% with mismatch repair deficiency (Royal 2010, Brahmer 2012, O'Reilly 2019, Bear 2020).
after: In a fictional comparison, inflamed and excluded fields each contain eight specified T-cell symbols, relocated from mainly within malignant regions to surrounding stroma; a desert field has two. Equal counts can conceal different locations. Region outlines do not prove a physical barrier, these counts do not describe all mononuclear cells used in stromal TIL scoring, and they cannot be converted to an sTIL area percentage. The example depicts neither lymph-node follicles nor tertiary lymphoid organization and supplies no clinical cutoff or response rate.

Routine pathology can score a defined infiltrate, multiplex imaging adds selected cell identities and coordinates, and mixed-tissue gene expression describes programmes without directly retaining each cell’s location. Report the preparation, section, sampled regions, staining and cell-assignment rules, regional variation, output and denominator. Descriptive labels, cells per area and method-defined stromal scores are different outputs. Sectioning and staining use finite tissue. Damage, staining error, incorrect boundaries and an unrepresentative region can limit the result. A research classifier needs separate validation for a clinical selection use.

In Loi’s pooled analysis of 2,148 early TNBC patients given anthracycline-based adjuvant chemotherapy with or without taxanes, each 10 percentage-point increase in stromal TILs was associated with iDFS HR 0.87 and OS HR 0.84. This is prognosis in that population, not proof of additional checkpoint-drug benefit by hot/cold category. Taube’s tissue study also supports coexistence of lymphocyte infiltration and induced inhibitory PD-L1; hot does not mean every later immune step succeeds.

Pancreatic examples have specific settings. Feig’s pancreatic mouse model connected FAP-positive fibroblast CXCL12 with T-cell exclusion; Yamamoto’s work identified autophagy-dependent class-I degradation and tested immune rescue in mice. These are not measurements of every human pancreatic tumour. Royal’s 27-person ipilimumab study reported no RECIST responses but one delayed regression after initial progression. O’Reilly’s 65-person metastatic study reported objective response rates of 3.1% with durvalumab plus tremelimumab and 0% with durvalumab alone, without meeting its expansion threshold. These historical studies do not establish a complete treatment-selection rule or prove that one molecular subgroup is the only possible responder population.

fields.before: A tumour where the immune cells arrive but are stopped at the edge, held back by scar tissue and signals such as TGF-β.
fields.after: Immune exclusion describes immune cells concentrated outside cancer-cell regions. Their distribution raises questions about access; it does not identify the barrier or a treatment that will overcome it.

fields.before: Immune exclusion describes a tumour where immune cells arrive but are stopped at the edge, held back by scar tissue and signals such as TGF-β. It is one of three immune phenotypes (inflamed, excluded and desert) and is associated with TGF-β-activated fibroblasts, dense extracellular matrix and abnormal vessels, as described in the TGF-β signalling and Tumour microenvironment (TME) pathways and the Hot vs cold tumours entry. It predicts poor response to checkpoint inhibitors in bladder, colorectal and pancreatic cancer, and the candidate targets are TGF-β, FAP, CXCL12/CXCR4 and VEGF / VEGFR. Readers meet the term in the hallmark Avoiding immune destruction, in the cold tumours pathway, and in the idea What actually holds T cells at the tumour border?
fields.after:
After priming, a T cell must be recruited, adhere to and leave a vessel, traverse stroma and reach relevant cancer cells. An excluded distribution records where cells were found. It does not establish why they stopped. A cell that has reached a target but is inhibited has a different measured problem, although access and functional failures can coexist.

Candidate mechanisms include recruitment signals, vascular interactions, matrix architecture, fibroblast signalling and myeloid-cell contacts. Their evidence comes from different cancers, human tissue studies and experimental models. A location measurement, causal perturbation and successful clinical intervention are different claims. Dense stroma alone does not diagnose exclusion or identify a safe way to reverse it.

before: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma: T cells are absent from the regions holding cancer cells, which are coated with CXCL12 secreted by FAP-positive fibroblasts; depleting those fibroblasts or blocking CXCR4 let T cells in and uncovered the effect of anti-PD-L1 in the mouse model (Feig 2013). The long-term survivors who escape this pattern have both abundant CD8 infiltrate and high-quality neoantigens, and lose those clones at metastasis (Balachandran 2017).
after: Harlin found six chemokines, including CCL5, CXCL9 and CXCL10, preferentially in T-cell-containing human melanoma metastases, with supporting migration experiments. In melanoma models, Mikucki found that CXCR3 supported intravascular arrest and extravasation of transferred CD8 effectors. These findings identify defined recruitment and vascular dependencies, not a universal explanation for every abnormal vessel. Spranger’s human melanoma association and mouse experiments connected tumour WNT/beta-catenin activity with deficient dendritic-cell recruitment and absent T-cell infiltration, a desert-like problem rather than necessarily an excluded rim. In their 2015 commentary on the mouse experiments, Spranger and Gajewski describe reduced CCL4 expression and failed recruitment of Batf3-lineage dendritic cells. This is a defined melanoma mechanism, not a universal explanation for every excluded tissue pattern.

In viable human lung-tumour slices, Salmon observed better T-cell movement in loose matrix, restricted movement in dense aligned matrix and increased cancer-cell contact after collagenase. Mariathasan associated stromal fibroblast TGF-beta signalling, exclusion and atezolizumab non-response in metastatic urothelial cancer; combined TGF-beta and PD-L1 blockade improved penetration and regression in mice. Peranzoni linked long macrophage-CD8 contacts and poor motility to exclusion in human lung squamous cancers, then used macrophage-directed treatment in mice to improve tumour-islet access. None of these model interventions establishes a beneficial breast-cancer regimen.

Hammerl’s spatial analysis of 681 TNBCs distinguished excluded, ignored and inflamed groups. Excluded samples showed collagen-10 deposits and TGF-beta/VEGF programmes; ignored samples showed either dense CD163-positive myeloid cells or WNT/PPAR-gamma programmes. The classifier also associated with anti-PD-1 response in a metastatic-TNBC phase-II trial. Gruosso separately associated stroma-restricted CD8 cells and stromal PD-L1 with poorer outcome. These associations do not prove the observed barrier caused resistance or that its removal helps a particular patient.

A chemokine can matter after entry. Chow found that CXCR3 and dendritic-cell-derived CXCL9 were required for productive anti-PD-1 responses in tumour-bearing mice but were not required for initial CD8 infiltration. This is different from Mikucki’s transferred-cell vascular-trafficking experiment. Name the tested step, model, stimulus and endpoint before treating the two studies as the same claim.

Multiplex imaging can separately count CD8 cells in stroma and malignant nests and measure distances. Bulk chemokine, fibroblast or TGF-beta RNA programmes lose direct location. A high stromal TIL area score can therefore coexist with exclusion. In a fictional comparison, collagen-rich stroma with peripheral CD8 cells and high TGF-beta suggests a different access question from sparse T cells with low recruiting chemokines. Both remain hypotheses requiring appropriate measurements and functional controls, rather than diagnoses from one image.

Feig’s pancreatic mouse model found T cells outside cancer-cell regions coated with CAF-derived CXCL12; fibroblast depletion or CXCR4 blockade improved access and revealed checkpoint-antibody activity in that model. Separately, Balachandran’s human pancreatic-cancer study associated combined neoantigen and CD8 features with long survival, detected relevant T-cell reactivity and observed selective loss of high-quality neoantigenic clones during metastatic progression. Those findings do not show that every long-term survivor overcame one specific physical exclusion barrier.

fields.before: Tumours come in three immune weathers: inflamed (T cells inside, checkpoint drugs work), excluded (T cells stuck at the edge), and desert (no T cells at all). Most common cancers are excluded or desert, and turning them 'hot' is the central problem of immunotherapy.
fields.after: Sparse T cells and T cells gathered outside malignant regions are different immune patterns. An inflamed tumour can still restrain its T cells, and a pattern alone does not select a treatment.

fields.before: Deserts arise from low antigenicity (low TMB, MHC loss), failed priming (few BATF3+ cDC1, low CCL4 because of tumour-intrinsic WNT/β-catenin signalling; PTEN loss; MYC-driven CD47/PD-L1), and absent chemokines (CXCL9/10 silenced by EZH2 and DNMT1). Exclusion arises from stroma: TGF-β-activated CAFs and dense collagen (Mariathasan 2018), CXCL12 from FAP+ fibroblasts, abnormal VEGF-driven vessels lacking adhesion molecules, and myeloid barriers. Inflamed tumours still fail through PD-L1, exhaustion and Tregs. Converters: radiotherapy and chemotherapy (immunogenic death, STING), oncolytic viruses and in situ vaccines, STING agonists (systemic versions disappointed), anti-VEGF and TGF-β blockade (bintrafusp alfa failed), FAP/CXCR4 targeting, epigenetic priming to restore chemokines, and antigen-independent killers (engagers, CAR-T) that do not need a hot tumour. Gene signatures (T-cell inflamed GEP, TIS) and spatial pathology grade the weather.
fields.after:
Immune deserts have few relevant T cells in the sampled regions; immune exclusion describes cells nearby with limited entry into malignant nests. Deficient antigen availability or priming, recruitment signals, vascular interactions and stromal access can produce different distributions. Tumour WNT/beta-catenin-associated loss of dendritic-cell recruitment is one model-supported route to absent infiltration. An inflamed pattern can coexist with induced inhibitory signals, regulatory cells and exhausted programmes.

These are hypotheses about distinct dependencies. The same cancer can contain different regions or sites and can change with treatment. Matrix or cell abundance, a mixed RNA signature and spatial counts are different measurements. A proposed converter or HLA-independent recognition system still needs target, access, function, safety and comparative outcome evidence. There is no universal conversion treatment or hot/cold cutoff implied by the framework.

fields.before: Three kinds of town: one where the police already patrol the streets (inflamed), one where they mill about outside a wall (excluded), and one with no police station at all (desert). Removing the officers' handcuffs (PD-1 blockade) only helps in the first; the second needs a gate, the third needs recruitment.
fields.after: Three maps of the same neighbourhood can show many lymphocytes among cancer cells, cells concentrated outside, or few cells in either region. The map describes location; it does not identify the cause or select a treatment. Different mechanisms can produce a similar pattern.

after: Antigen-release, vaccination and local immune-stimulation approaches investigate different missing inputs. Local inflammation or an interferon signal does not by itself establish distant cancer control.

Vascular and stromal approaches investigate access in defined tumour systems. A location pattern alone does not show which barrier is causal or which intervention will change outcomes. In Feig’s pancreatic mouse model, CXCR4 blockade improved T-cell access; this is not established human benefit.

Chemokine or dendritic-cell recruitment can be tested with spatial measurements and controlled perturbations. A response signature or altered cell count alone does not establish restoration of the entire immune response.

Engagers, engineered cells and vaccines still require suitable targets, access and function. Their recognition mechanisms differ, and none can be assumed to bypass every cause of an immune-poor pattern.

fields.before: Neoadjuvant therapy is treatment given before surgery, adjuvant therapy is treatment given after it, and perioperative therapy is both. Neoadjuvant treatment shrinks tumours and shows whether the drug works in the living patient; adjuvant treatment aims to kill microscopic disease left behind.
fields.after: Neoadjuvant treatment is given before surgery, adjuvant treatment after it, and perioperative treatment around both phases. The benefit and risks of the timing depend on the disease and complete regimen.

fields.before: Neoadjuvant, adjuvant and perioperative therapy mean treatment given before surgery, after surgery, or both; pre-operative and post-operative are the everyday equivalents. Neoadjuvant treatment shrinks tumours, tests drug sensitivity in the living patient through pathologic complete response and can allow surgery to be de-escalated, while adjuvant treatment aims to kill micrometastases. Immunotherapy appears to work better neoadjuvantly, as NADINA and CheckMate 816 suggested, because the primary tumour is still present to supply antigen. The term is anchored to KEYNOTE-522 and referenced by KEYNOTE-671 and SWOG S1801, by the Colorectal, Gastric, Oesophageal, Bladder & urothelial and Head and neck cancer entries, and by the related term Major pathological response (MPR).
fields.after:
Neoadjuvant, adjuvant and perioperative describe timing before surgery, after surgery or across both phases. Neoadjuvant therapy can aim to reduce disease before an operation and provides response information from treated tissue. Adjuvant therapy aims to reduce risk from disease that may remain. A pathological response and a later clinical outcome are different endpoints.

Timing comparisons need the actual population, intervention and comparator. Liu’s two mouse breast-cancer models supported testing preoperative immunotherapy, not a universal human timing rule or proof that retained tumour antigen explains every clinical result. KEYNOTE-522 assigned a complete before-and-after pembrolizumab regimen against its comparator; that design does not independently randomize the two phases and cannot isolate each phase’s contribution.

fields.before: Natural killer cells patrol for cells that have lost their identity papers (MHC-I) or that display stress flags. Cancers that hide from T cells by dropping MHC-I become visible to NK cells, unless they also shed the stress flags, wrap themselves in a second inhibitory badge (HLA-E), or soak the neighbourhood in TGF-β.
fields.after: Natural killer cells integrate several receptor inputs. Loss of an inhibitory self signal can matter, but target ligands, prior education and the cell’s current state also affect whether it kills.

fields.before: NK activation integrates inhibitory signals from KIRs and NKG2A (binding classical HLA-A/B/C and HLA-E respectively; 'missing self' when MHC-I is lost) against activating signals from NKG2D (MICA/B, ULBP1-6, induced by DNA damage and oncogenes), DNAM-1 (CD155, CD112), NKp30 (B7-H6), NKp46, and CD16 (FcγRIIIa, mediating ADCC by IgG1 antibodies such as trastuzumab and cetuximab). Killing is by perforin/granzyme and death ligands; IFN-γ recruits and licenses the adaptive response. Tumour escape: proteolytic shedding of MICA/B (ADAM10/17), HLA-E upregulation engaging NKG2A (monalizumab, mixed results), TIGIT and PVRIG competing with DNAM-1 for CD155, TGF-β and adenosine downregulating NKG2D, platelet cloaking of CTCs. NK cells are central to clearing circulating tumour cells and dormant cells and to controlling MHC-I-negative escape variants after checkpoint or CAR-T therapy. Therapeutics: CAR-NK (cord blood, iPSC-derived, off the shelf, low CRS), NK engagers (CD16×target), IL-15 superagonists (nogapendekin alfa approved in NMIBC), anti-NKG2A, antibody afucosylation to boost ADCC.
fields.after:
Natural killer (NK) receptors are encoded in the germ line rather than assembled by the T-cell receptor’s somatic rearrangement process. They integrate complementary activating inputs with inhibitory signals; this is more complex than adding fixed on/off switches. Inhibitory motifs can recruit SHP phosphatases and suppress early activation, while several activating receptors signal through adaptors. Repertoire, receptor variants, prior education, cytokines and the target context matter. Some receptors also occur on T cells, and HLA-related recognition can depend on the bound peptide.

Inhibitory KIR2DL1 and KIR2DL2/3 recognize subsets of HLA-C; KIR3DL1 recognizes the Bw4 epitope on class-I molecules. Activating KIRs also exist, with variant-dependent ligands: curated examples include KIR2DS1/HLA-C and KIR3DS1/peptide-free HLA-F. CD94/NKG2A is inhibitory and reads peptide-loaded HLA-E; CD94/NKG2C is activating and bound HLA-E with lower affinity than NKG2A in the recombinant-protein study. CMV seropositivity was associated with NKG2C-rich repertoires in healthy donors. These are defined receptor-ligand findings, not interchangeable switches.

after: NKG2D is activating and recognizes stress-related MICA, MICB and ULBP ligands; it also occurs on CD8 and gamma-delta T cells. NKp30, NKp44 and NKp46 are natural cytotoxicity receptors with adaptor-dependent signalling. Activating DNAM-1/CD226 recognizes CD155 and CD112; inhibitory TIGIT recognizes this ligand system as well. CD16 recognizes antibody Fc and can supply antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity. Fc design changes that interaction. Receptor identity is different from the cancer antigen bound by an antibody, and Long’s review describes conditions in which CD16 can activate resting NK cells without the complementary inputs required by several other tested receptors. Shared ligand recognition does not by itself measure relative affinity, competitive occupancy or which receptor input dominates in a particular cell and target pair.

Education tunes responsiveness. NK cells with matched self-HLA inhibitory interactions can be more responsive to later activating stimuli, while unmatched cells can be hyporesponsive. In Juelke’s human-cell experiments, cytokine-stimulated hyporesponsive cells acquired competence when they acquired KIR in the presence of its cognate MHC. This is not a fixed panel present identically on every NK cell. Removing one inhibitory HLA interaction is not necessarily removal of all restraints or a sufficient activation signal.

Groh found reduced NKG2D on tumour-infiltrating and matched blood T cells in people with cancer, associated with circulating soluble tumour-derived MICA and impaired tumour-antigen-specific T-cell responsiveness. That human observation should not silently become a measurement of every NK cell. André’s NKG2A-blockade work supported NK and CD8 activity in laboratory and mouse systems and reported an early combination-trial signal. Those observations did not establish comparative clinical efficacy.

INTERLINK-1 tested monalizumab plus cetuximab against placebo plus cetuximab after checkpoint therapy and platinum progression in recurrent/metastatic head-and-neck cancer. The HPV-unrelated primary analysis set contained 216 participants, randomized 2:1. Median overall survival was 8.8 versus 8.6 months, HR 1.00 (95% CI 0.66 to 1.54); the trial met its prespecified futility criterion. This negative comparison does not support a general claim of clinical success for NKG2A blockade.

Flow cytometry measures receptor proteins on defined viable populations; KIR/HLA genotyping identifies possible pairs; tissue protein or RNA tests ask about ligands; a controlled NK-target assay measures killing. A fictional target lacking all measured HLA restraints but lacking measured activating ligands need not be killed. An antibody engaging CD16 supplies a further hypothesis to test. Receptor expression, degranulation, target death, tumour entry and patient benefit remain separate measurements.

An activating-KIR label does not imply that the gene is present in every person or that its ligand is interchangeable with another receptor’s. The breast stromal TIL method estimates the area occupied by mononuclear inflammatory cells, including lymphocytes and plasma cells, as a percentage of eligible tumour-associated stroma. It is not the percentage of all cells, a CD8-cell count or the fraction of cancer cells being killed.

Define the eligible region and treatment setting before estimating the percentage. Use the specified exclusions for normal structures, in-situ disease, necrosis, crush damage and biopsy-site changes, and assess the region overall rather than only its hottest spot. A prognostic association does not establish added benefit from a particular treatment.

In the pooled analysis of 2,148 early-stage TNBC patients given anthracycline-based chemotherapy with or without taxanes, each 10 percentage-point increase in pretreatment stromal TILs corresponded to an adjusted invasive disease-free survival hazard ratio of 0.87 (95% confidence interval 0.83 to 0.91) and overall survival hazard ratio of 0.84 (0.79 to 0.89). These associations do not establish an added pembrolizumab benefit by TIL level.

Among 906 TNBC patients from six neoadjuvant chemotherapy trials, pathological complete response occurred in 80 of 260 with low TILs (0% to 10%), 117 of 373 with intermediate TILs (11% to 59%) and 136 of 273 with high TILs (at least 60%): about 31%, 31% and 50%. These categories describe that analysis and are not universal treatment cutoffs.

Fictional area exercise: region A has 4 units of eligible stroma with 0.4 occupied by infiltrate; region B has 1 unit with 0.6 occupied. Pooled occupied area is (0.4 + 0.6)/(4 + 1) = 20%. Averaging the regional percentages without area weighting gives (10% + 60%)/2 = 35%. Immune surveillance concerns immune control of transformed cells. Immunoediting adds that immune pressure can alter which cancer populations persist. Elimination, equilibrium and escape describe processes that can coexist or occur independently, not a mandatory three-stage calendar. Shankaran’s genetically defined mouse experiments support lymphocyte and interferon-gamma contributions to control and selection. They do not measure what fraction of all human cancers immunity prevents.

Koebel used immune perturbation in chemical-carcinogenesis mouse models to demonstrate equilibrium; a quiet scan alone is not such an experiment. Matsushita combined sequencing, antigen recognition and immune comparisons in mouse sarcoma to support selection of pre-existing antigen-distinct clones. This is different from T cells creating every mutation that appears later.

Luksza followed 70 pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas from 15 people longitudinally over ten years, comparing primary and recurrent tumours and modelling neoantigen quality and clonal fitness. Long-term survivors had stronger primary T-cell activity and recurrent tumours with fewer high-quality neoantigens under the model. This is human cohort and modelling evidence, not a vaccine experiment or direct observation of every selection event. Treatment and sampling history and model assumptions remain relevant.

In a fictional immune-pressure comparison, both arms begin with A/B counts of 80/20. Later, the control has 160/40 and the pressure arm 10/40. B is 20% versus 80% of the later populations, although its later count is 40 in both. Recognition and comparable conditions are separate evidence; a larger share does not mean that pressure created more B cells. This example is distinct from 900/100 becoming 90/90, where B’s share rises while its count falls.

An editing claim combines longitudinal populations or antigens, recognition or functional assays and relevant comparisons. One immune-rich sample, negative blood test or model cannot assign an individual postoperative phase, explain every recurrence or forecast personal risk; different lesions can face different pressures.

fields.after: agretopicity
term
Agretopicity
Agretopicity compares predicted binding of a tumour's altered and normal peptides to immune display molecules. It can help rank candidates; actual display and immune recognition need separate tests.

Agretopicity compares two predicted binding scores for the same stretch of protein: the mutant peptide carrying the tumour's altered amino acid, and its wild-type counterpart from the normal genome, each scored against a person's human leukocyte antigen (HLA) class I molecules by prediction software. Duan and colleagues named the numerical difference in NetMHC scores between mutated and unmutated sequences the differential agretopic index (DAI). Duan subtracted the wild-type NetMHC score from the mutant score. Some groups use a ratio instead, and sign conventions and subtraction order differ between papers, so a DAI value cannot be compared across pipelines without reading each one's definition.

Two separate ideas sit behind the measure. First, a mutation at a position the HLA groove grips can create a new anchor residue and change binding, potentially changing presentation; Duan and colleagues found that neoepitopes mutated to create new anchor residues, together with greater predicted rigidity of the peptide and HLA complex, identified protective neoepitopes with relatively high accuracy in mouse tumours (the CMS5 and Meth A mouse tumours). Second, reasoning rather than a finding of the cited papers: a peptide that normal tissue never displayed well may not have had its reactive T cells removed by self-tolerance, so a high value is sometimes read as a proxy for an intact T-cell repertoire against that target.

A high value does not require strong absolute binding. In that mouse work the protective neoepitopes produced CD8-dependent immunity although their affinity for the mouse class I molecule H-2Kd was orders of magnitude weaker than the conventional 500 nanomolar threshold, which is part of the argument for ranking on the mutant-versus-wild-type comparison rather than on absolute predicted affinity alone.

Ghorani’s retrospective human analysis included 66 lung adenocarcinomas and 72 melanomas from The Cancer Genome Atlas, plus three immunotherapy-treated cohorts containing 131 melanoma patients in total and 31 with non-small-cell lung cancer. Mean DAI correlated with overall survival in three of five cohorts, with the reported effect for clonal rather than subclonal peptides. The authors reported evidence of superiority over nonsynonymous mutational and neoantigen burden in these analyses, not a universally superior clinical predictor. Mean DAI also correlated with immune-infiltration measures in melanoma (P = 0.027) and lung adenocarcinoma (P = 0.024), whereas mutational and neoantigen burden did not. The association with survival was not uniform: P = 0.068 in the TCGA melanoma cohort and P = 0.003 in one treated melanoma cohort. These population associations and the animal protection findings are different evidence tiers. Neither prospectively demonstrates that selecting a vaccine by DAI improves clinical outcomes.

The 2020 Tumor Neoantigen Selection Alliance study tested which peptide features predict immunogenicity: 608 predicted epitopes were assessed for T-cell binding in patient-matched samples, and a model integrating peptide features linked to presentation and recognition filtered out 98% of non-immunogenic peptides at a precision above 0.70, then held in an independent cohort of 310 epitopes (Wells and colleagues). Its abstract does not say which features entered the model, so this record does not claim that the study supported or rejected agretopicity.

after: Agretopicity is not immunogenicity. It is a predicted property of a peptide and HLA pair, while immunogenicity is a measured T-cell response; prediction, presentation and recognition are three separate questions, and agretopicity speaks only to the first. Whether a peptide is actually displayed is a separate measurement (immunopeptidomics), and whether T cells respond to it is another again.

Agretopicity is not absolute binding strength: the reference is the peptide's own wild-type version. It is also different from sequence self-similarity, which asks how much a peptide resembles normal human sequences more broadly. The Duan and Ghorani studies concern class I; their findings do not validate a class-II ranking rule. HLA is the human form of the major histocompatibility complex, called MHC in the mouse experiments.

The score is computed from sequence and binding predictions for the alleles supplied by HLA typing. Retain the peptide windows, allele, predictor and version, both scores, units and subtraction or ratio rule. Sign conventions differ, so a larger number in one pipeline need not match another's scale. Computation adds no tissue assay, but depends on the sequence and typing inputs. On a design board it sits beside expression, clonality and measured presentation. Absolute affinity alone does not reveal how much the mutant differs from its wild-type counterpart. Neither comparison proves escape from tolerance, natural presentation or a useful T-cell response. Different predictors can give different estimates for the same peptide pair.

adaptive-immune-resistance
term
Adaptive immune resistance

An immune attack can induce its own restraint: signals from responding T cells raise inhibitory proteins on nearby cells. This induced defence differs from resistance acquired after a treatment response.

The sequence proposed by Taube and colleagues and mapped in more detail since is a loop. A T cell recognises a tumour peptide on HLA and releases interferon gamma; the interferon acts through the Janus kinases JAK1 and JAK2 in nearby tumour and immune cells; PD-L1 rises; PD-L1 binds PD-1 on the T cell and damps it. In melanoma cell lines, Garcia-Diaz and colleagues found that the interferon gamma, JAK1 and JAK2, STAT1, STAT2 and STAT3, IRF1 axis primarily regulates PD-L1, with IRF1 binding the PD-L1 promoter, and biopsies from patients with melanoma showed enrichment of that interferon signature and of STAT and IRF1 target genes in tumours that responded to anti-PD-1 treatment.

PD-L1 is not the only brake that follows the attack. Spranger and colleagues found in human melanoma that the T-cell-inflamed tumours were the ones with high indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase (IDO), PD-L1 and regulatory T cells, and in mice that all three depended on CD8 T cells being present: IDO and PD-L1 through interferon gamma, and regulatory T cells through CCR4-binding chemokines with some induced proliferation. Their reading was that these pathways are driven by the immune response rather than orchestrated by the cancer cells.

Evidence from tissue. In human melanocytic lesions, 98% of PD-L1-positive (B7-H1-positive) tumours had tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes compared with 28% of PD-L1-negative tumours; positive melanocytes sat almost always immediately next to lymphocytes, and interferon gamma was detected at the interface but not in PD-L1-negative tumours (Taube and colleagues). The same colocalisation appeared in inflamed benign naevi, which fits PD-L1 as a response to tissue inflammation. In triple-negative breast cancer, Gruosso and colleagues described an immunoreactive group whose tumours had granzyme B-positive CD8 T cells inside cancer-cell regions, a type 1 interferon signature and elevated IDO and PD-L1, the pattern adaptive resistance predicts; that is an association in tissue and not a direct test of the loop. The alternative, called innate or constitutive resistance, is PD-L1 driven by the cancer cell's own signalling regardless of T cells.

A functionally important loss of JAK1 or JAK2 can impair the tumour cell response to interferon gamma. In four people with metastatic melanoma that relapsed on anti-PD-1 treatment, two relapse samples carried loss-of-function JAK1 or JAK2 mutations with deletion of the remaining normal allele, and truncating JAK1 or JAK2 mutations left the cells unresponsive to interferon gamma (Zaretsky and colleagues). The JAK2-deficient relapse cells lost interferon-gamma-induced PD-L1 and class-I increases but retained responses to interferon alfa and beta. In engineered melanoma cells, JAK1 or JAK2 loss did not abolish recognition by the tested NY-ESO-1-specific T cells. Loss of inducibility is therefore different from absence of all baseline recognition. This selected series does not estimate a frequency for all cancers.

perioperative-immune-window
term
Perioperative immune window

Surgery and recovery can temporarily change immune activity. Studies of blood or laboratory markers differ from trials measuring recurrence, and a marker change alone does not show better cancer outcomes.

Several things happen at once around an operation. Reviews describe a stress response in which injury and stress release catecholamines, prostaglandins and cortisol, and in which a short pro-inflammatory phase is followed by a prolonged anti-inflammatory phase; natural killer (NK) cells are severely affected in that period, and sympathetic stress factors, mediators including interleukin 6 and transforming growth factor beta, and myeloid-derived suppressor cells have been proposed as mediators (Horowitz and colleagues; Angka and colleagues). Wound healing adds repair signals, and anaesthesia and pain control add their own possible effects: the breast cancer anaesthesia trials were built on the premise that the surgical stress response, volatile anaesthetic and opioids impair host defence and that regional anaesthesia with propofol ameliorates all three. Most of this mechanistic evidence comes from blood measurements in patients and from mouse models, so whether the changes alter recurrence in people is a separate question that randomised trials answer best.

A real, short-lived shift in NK-cell function and suppressive signals is described by human blood studies and mouse work, which do not measure recurrence. Anaesthetic choice in breast cancer surgery was tested in two randomised trials. Sessler and colleagues analysed 2,108 women (13 hospitals, 8 countries) given regional anaesthesia with paravertebral blocks and propofol or general anaesthesia with sevoflurane and opioid analgesia: recurrence occurred in 102 of 1,043 (10%) and 111 of 1,065 (10%), hazard ratio 0.97 (95% CI 0.74 to 1.28), median follow-up 36 months; the trial stopped after a preplanned futility boundary was crossed, and persistent incisional pain did not differ. Enlund and colleagues (the Cancer and Anaesthesia study, designed to detect an advantage of at least five percentage points for propofol) recruited 1,764 women, of whom 1,670 remained for analysis, and found five-year survival of 773 of 841 (91.9%) with propofol and 764 of 829 (92.2%) with sevoflurane, hazard ratio 1.03 (95% CI 0.73 to 1.44). Neither trial detected an advantage in its specified clinical endpoint. Their confidence intervals do not prove that all anaesthetic approaches are equivalent; keep the agents, breast-cancer population, endpoint and follow-up attached.

Blocking the stress signals is a different question. In a randomised, placebo-controlled biomarker trial of 38 women with early breast cancer, 11 days of propranolol (a beta-blocker) with etodolac (a COX-2 inhibitor) from 5 days before surgery was well tolerated and changed tumour gene expression (less epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, fewer tumour-infiltrating monocytes, more tumour-infiltrating B cells) and blood markers (smaller presurgical rises in interleukin 6 and C-reactive protein) (Shaashua and colleagues). Recurrence was not an endpoint, so this is a biomarker result and not fewer recurrences.

Timing of immunotherapy is another open question. In two mouse models of spontaneously metastatic breast cancer, immunotherapy given before removal of the primary tumour eradicated distant metastases more effectively than the same treatment given after, with sustained peripheral tumour-specific immune responses underpinning the outcome (Liu and colleagues). That supports testing the idea in people; it is not a human result. The KEYNOTE-522 regimen gives pembrolizumab with chemotherapy before surgery and alone after it to the same patients, so by design it cannot separate the benefit of the two phases (inference from the trial design).

cd4-t-cell-subsets
term
CD4 T-cell subsets
CD4 T cells can develop different response programmes. Signals, gene activity and measured function help describe a programme; a single marker does not establish what the cell does.

CD4 T-cell subsets are differentiation programmes shaped by antigen recognition, cytokines and gene regulation. Conventional naive CD4 cells recognize peptide-HLA class II during priming, often on dendritic cells. Th1, Th2, Th17, follicular helper and regulatory programmes have characteristic signals, transcription factors and outputs, but these are not permanent job titles or mutually exclusive functional tests. The original Th1/Th2 distinction came from mouse clones in 1986; human tissue can contain mixed programmes.

CD4 help can improve the magnitude and quality of a CD8 response. Bennett’s experiments showed that CD40 signalling on antigen-presenting cells could replace CD4 help in a defined cross-priming system. Cella found that CD40 ligation increased dendritic-cell IL-12, ICAM-1, CD80 and CD86 and their T-cell-stimulating capacity. These support one licensing mechanism, not a requirement that every response follows an identical route.

Alspach’s mouse-tumour work required tumour-antigen-specific CD4 and CD8 responses even when the cancer cells lacked class-II molecules; tumour expression of class-II-restricted antigens was needed at the successful rejection site. In Ott’s phase-I melanoma vaccine trial, six people received personal neoantigens. CD4 responses targeted 58 of 97 neoantigens (60%) and CD8 responses 15 (16%). Four of six had no recurrence at 25 months, but the small uncontrolled study did not isolate clinical efficacy.

In untreated human breast tumours, Gu-Trantien found CXCL13-producing Tfh cells mainly in tertiary-lymphoid-structure germinal centres and an eight-gene signature associated with survival or preoperative-chemotherapy response. That is a prognostic association. DeNardo’s mouse mammary-cancer experiments showed a different possibility: IL-4-producing CD4 cells shaped macrophages that promoted invasion and lung metastasis. Subset identity therefore needs tissue, timing and measured-function context.

after: A transcription-factor stain is a clue to a programme, not a function test. In defined human cultures, Tran and colleagues induced high FOXP3 expression without suppressive function. Human colorectal tumours also contained functionally distinct FOXP3-positive populations (Saito 2016). T-bet expression alone does not measure interferon-gamma release, and a bulk Th1-related RNA signature is not a count of one cell type. Neither Th1 nor Th2 identity alone establishes benefit or harm across tissue, timing and tumour contexts.

How subsets are measured. Flow cytometry can stain transcription factors and, after stimulation, cytokines inside cells; single-cell RNA sequencing assigns programmes by gene expression; tissue staining for CXCL13 or FOXP3 adds location. Each method defines subsets by its own markers, so labels may not match across studies.

Worked example (inference). A vaccine study reports strong interferon gamma release from CD4 T cells after stimulation with a vaccine peptide, but no CD8 response. That is not necessarily a failure: Th1-like CD4 cells can license dendritic cells and help CD8 responses, and mouse data show CD4 cells are needed for rejection. The result shows a CD4 response under assay conditions; recognition of the tumour and any benefit need separate evidence.

CD4 does not mean helper-only. Oh and colleagues studied 30,604 T cells from seven bladder-cancer patients and found clonally expanded cytotoxic CD4 states; controlled assays demonstrated MHC-class-II-dependent killing of autologous tumour cells and inhibition by regulatory T cells. This human evidence has a defined cancer, assay and target context. It does not make every CD4 cell cytotoxic or replace the separate helper and regulatory measurements.

Th1 programmes are associated with IL-12 and interferon-gamma signalling and the transcription factor T-bet. Cells can produce interferon gamma and IL-2 and support macrophage and CD8 responses against intracellular microbes, including the development of memory responses. A T-bet stain alone does not demonstrate any one of those outputs.

Th2 differentiation in the systems reviewed by Zhu involved IL-4 and IL-2, with GATA3 and characteristic IL-4, IL-5 and IL-13 production. These programmes are studied in parasite and allergic responses. This functional context does not make Th2 identity uniformly harmful or beneficial in a tumour.

Th17 programmes include ROR-gamma-t and IL-17A, IL-17F and IL-22 outputs. Zhu’s 2010 review described efficient TGF-beta/IL-6-driven differentiation in specified cultures and a later role for IL-23 in development or maintenance. Human STAT3-deficiency observations linked deficient Th17 development with susceptibility to bacterial and fungal infections. Culture steering conditions and barrier-defence associations are not a universal human differentiation recipe or an automatic tumour-effect prediction.

Follicular helper programmes include BCL6 and the CXCR5 receptor that supports follicular location, and help germinal-centre B cells, including through IL-21. Human breast-tumour Tfh cells can produce CXCL13. Zhu’s 2010 discussion of IL-6/IL-21 culture conditions described uncertainty at that time; neither those conditions nor one marker define every Tfh cell or its function.

Regulatory programmes help restrain responses and maintain tolerance. FOXP3 is a central regulator, and TGF-beta/IL-2 support induced differentiation in specified experimental systems. IL-10, TGF-beta and CTLA-4-associated interactions can contribute to regulation in context. These are not exclusive outputs of one programme, and the human FOXP3 studies above explain why marker presence needs a separate suppression assay.

after: Immune escape can involve loss of a targeted antigen, altered HLA alleles or processing, defective inducible signalling, inhibition after entry or impaired access. Anagnostou found loss of putative neoantigens in checkpoint-resistant lung tumours with accompanying T-cell evidence. McGranahan described allele-specific HLA loss in lung cancer evolution. Montesion’s commercial pan-cancer genomic series contained 83,644 samples with HLA-I loss of heterozygosity in 17%; this assay-defined pan-cancer observation is not a breast-specific prevalence. Allele loss differs from reversible expression change or a B2M defect affecting class-I surface display.

In Zaretsky’s selected four-person melanoma relapse series, two cases had JAK1 or JAK2 loss-of-function changes with loss of the normal allele and another had a truncating B2M change. The JAK2-deficient relapse cells failed to increase interferon-gamma signalling, PD-L1 and class I while retaining interferon-alfa/beta responsiveness. Engineered JAK1- or JAK2-deficient melanoma cells were still recognized by the tested NY-ESO-1-specific T cells. Baseline display, inducibility, recognition and killing are separate dependencies; neither a JAK variant nor detectable HLA alone answers all of them.

In a fictional controlled comparison, both cultures have baseline class I; only the control increases its signal and surface display after interferon gamma. The candidate retains an interferon-alfa response, and restoring JAK2 restores the tested gamma response. With matched handling, viability and restoration controls, this supports a model-specific JAK2-dependent inducibility defect. It is not proof of a particular displayed peptide, safe clinical rescue, tumour access or useful killing. JAK1 and JAK2 have different interferon dependencies.

Treatment can select a pre-existing population and new changes can arise. Earlier specimens, retained alleles, expression, stimulation and controlled functional comparisons help test an escape explanation. Different sites may have different bottlenecks; several mechanisms may coexist. Blood tumour DNA alone does not identify a particular escape route. A proposed HLA-independent recognizer or combination still needs its own target, access, function and safety evidence, and a restored laboratory endpoint does not establish clinical benefit.

rows.beforeLiteral: ["Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma is the archetypal cold tumour: T cells exist but are held at the margin by CXCL12 from FAP-positive fibroblasts (Feig 2013) and MHC class I is degraded by autophagy (Yamamoto 2020), so single-agent ipilimumab (0 of 27), anti-PD-L1 (0 of 14 pancreatic patients) and durvalumab with or without tremelimumab (3.1% and 0% of 65) all failed; the only responsive group is the 1 to 2% with mismatch repair deficiency (Royal 2010, Brahmer 2012, O'Reilly 2019, Bear 2020)."]
after: Pancreatic examples have specific settings. Feig’s pancreatic mouse model connected FAP-positive fibroblast CXCL12 with T-cell exclusion; Yamamoto’s work identified autophagy-dependent class-I degradation and tested immune rescue in mice. These are not measurements of every human pancreatic tumour. Royal’s 27-person ipilimumab study reported no RECIST responses but one delayed regression after initial progression. O’Reilly’s 65-person metastatic study reported objective response rates of 3.1% with durvalumab plus tremelimumab and 0% with durvalumab alone, without meeting its expansion threshold. These historical studies do not establish a complete treatment-selection rule or prove that one molecular subgroup is the only possible responder population.

rows.beforeLiteral: ["Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma: T cells are absent from the regions holding cancer cells, which are coated with CXCL12 secreted by FAP-positive fibroblasts; depleting those fibroblasts or blocking CXCR4 let T cells in and uncovered the effect of anti-PD-L1 in the mouse model (Feig 2013). The long-term survivors who escape this pattern have both abundant CD8 infiltrate and high-quality neoantigens, and lose those clones at metastasis (Balachandran 2017)."]
after: Feig’s pancreatic mouse model found T cells outside cancer-cell regions coated with CAF-derived CXCL12; fibroblast depletion or CXCR4 blockade improved access and revealed checkpoint-antibody activity in that model. Separately, Balachandran’s human pancreatic-cancer study associated combined neoantigen and CD8 features with long survival, detected relevant T-cell reactivity and observed selective loss of high-quality neoantigenic clones during metastatic progression. Those findings do not show that every long-term survivor overcame one specific physical exclusion barrier.
